🚨 DENIED OR UNDERPAID: WHICH IS COSTING YOUR PRACTICE MORE?

A denied claim is easy to recognize—the payer refuses payment, your team receives $0, and the lost revenue appears immediately.

An underpaid claim can be harder to detect. The payer sends a partial payment, the account may appear settled, and the remaining balance can quietly go unnoticed.

Both problems weaken your revenue cycle, but repeated underpayments may create a larger hidden financial loss over time.

🔴 DENIED CLAIMS

A denied claim receives no payment until the issue is corrected, appealed, or resubmitted. Common causes include:

✅ Incorrect or missing patient information
✅ Coding and modifier errors
✅ Eligibility or authorization problems
✅ Medical-necessity disputes
✅ Duplicate or late claim submissions
✅ Missing clinical documentation

🟢 UNDERPAID CLAIMS

An underpaid claim receives payment—but less than the amount allowed under the payer contract. Common causes include:

✅ Incorrect fee-schedule application
✅ Bundling or downcoding errors
✅ Improper contractual adjustments
✅ Missing modifiers or units
✅ Incorrect patient-responsibility calculations
✅ Payer processing discrepancies

💡 WHY UNDERPAYMENTS ARE OFTEN MISSED

Because money was received, the claim may not receive the same attention as a full denial. Without regular payment-posting reviews, contract comparisons, and variance analysis, small shortages can accumulate across hundreds of claims.

A strong revenue recovery process should monitor both:

📌 Denial reasons and appeal deadlines
📌 Expected versus actual reimbursement
📌 Contractual adjustment accuracy
📌 Recurring payer payment patterns
📌 Unresolved and aging balances
📌 Appeal and corrected-claim outcomes

Whose network are you actually in?

Most dentists can name the PPOs they signed. Far fewer can name every entity now pricing their claims off those signatures.

That gap has a mechanism behind it. Provider network contracts are commonly leased — a payer grants a third party access to the contracted fee schedule. Third-party administrators sit in the same category. One agreement, several parties downstream, all pricing off the same page.

Some states regulate the practice. Michigan's law, MCL 500.3406aa, took effect in 2023 and requires a contracting entity — the definition expressly includes third-party administrators — to:

disclose in writing, at contract entry or renewal, all third parties with access;
-maintain a public website list of those third parties, updated at least every 30 days and dated;
-have third parties identify the discount's source on remittance advices and explanations of payment where a discount is taken, subject to carve-outs;
-provide a copy of the provider network contract relied on in adjudicating a claim within 30 days of a written request from the provider;
-and honor a provider's decision to decline third-party access, without canceling the contract over it.

More than a dozen states regulate network leasing in some form, and the specifics differ state by state. Treat Michigan as one worked example. Confirm what applies where you practice.

What applies everywhere: the ADA's pre-signing checklist tells dentists to ask about the "affiliates" clause by name, and to obtain and carefully review all attachments, exhibits, appendices and undisclosed documents before signing.

A practice carrying 25–35% write-offs deserves to know which contracts produced them. Start with 60 days of EOBs and a highlighter.

We walk practice owners through this audit as part of the groundwork for going fee-for-service — because a contract you've never read is a contract you can't weigh.

items.postText:
External audits are expensive.

Internal audits are free — and if you build the habit, you will rarely need the expensive kind.

Here is a simple quarterly internal billing audit framework that any practice can implement:

📋 Step 1: Pull a random sample of 20–25 paid claims from the prior quarter across your top 5 CPT codes

📋 Step 2: For each claim, verify:
   → Was the diagnosis code appropriate for the service billed?
   → Does the documentation in the medical record support the E&M level or procedure code?
   → Were modifiers used correctly and consistently?
   → Was the claim submitted to the correct payer with the correct fee schedule?
   → Was the payment received consistent with the contracted rate?

📋 Step 3: For each claim, verify the same for one denied claim in the same code range
   → What was the denial reason?
   → Was it preventable?
   → Was an appeal filed? Was it successful?

📋 Step 4: Compile findings by error category — documentation gaps, coding errors, payer billing rule violations, modifier misuse

📋 Step 5: Build a corrective action item for each error category — a training note, a workflow change, or a documentation template update

This process takes 3–4 hours per quarter. It costs nothing. And it catches patterns that would otherwise compound into thousands of dollars in denied or underpaid claims.

At David Medical Solutions, we conduct quarterly internal audit training for billing teams and provide the audit tools and templates to make this a permanent practice.

📩 Ask about quarterly internal audit training at davidmedicalsol.com
#InternalAudit #MedicalBilling #BillingTraining #StaffTraining #RCM #DavidMedicalSolutions

🚨 A DME Claim Can Be Paid and Still Be Underpaid

💡 DME Underpayments:
💰 In DME medical billing, receiving a payment does not always mean the claim was reimbursed correctly. A claim can be processed and paid while the actual reimbursement is lower than what should have been expected under the applicable contract or payer rules.

🔎 Payment Posting Is Only the First Step:
📋 Posting the payment tells you what the payer actually paid. DME payment analysis helps determine whether that payment matches the expected reimbursement.

🧾 Compare the Details:
📊 Review the allowed amount, paid amount, contractual adjustment, patient responsibility, units, HCPCS code, modifiers, and payer explanation. Small differences can reveal an underpayment that might otherwise be overlooked.

📑 Read the EOB/ERA:
🔍 The DME EOB or ERA can provide important information about how the payer processed the claim, including adjustments, reductions, bundling, or other payment decisions.

⚙️ Check Contractual Expectations:
📈 When applicable, compare the payer's reimbursement against the contracted rate, fee schedule, or other applicable payment terms. The goal is to determine whether the payment aligns with the expected reimbursement.

⏳ Don't Let Small Underpayments Accumulate:
💡 A small discrepancy on one claim may seem insignificant. Across hundreds of DME claims, however, repeated underpayments can create substantial revenue leakage.

📊 Track Patterns:
🔎 Underpayments should be analyzed by payer, HCPCS code, modifier, product category, and reimbursement pattern where appropriate. Repeated discrepancies may indicate a broader issue rather than an isolated claim.

🔗 A Strong DME Payment Review Process:

Payment Posted → EOB/ERA Reviewed → Expected vs. Actual Compared → Variance Identified → Root Cause Checked → Corrective Action

🎯 The Key Takeaway:
“Paid” doesn't always mean “paid correctly.”

Effective DME AR management includes identifying underpayments—not just unpaid claims. Regular payment analysis can help uncover revenue leakage and ensure reimbursement is being reviewed as carefully as claim denials.

Can You Spot an Underpaid Claim?

Before anyone comments that this is a marketing post, let me address that upfront.

Yes, I'm a Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner, Family Nurse Practitioner, Certified Professional Medical Auditor (CPMA), Certified Professional Coder (CPC), and Certified Professional Biller (CPB).

Yes, I own a medical billing company in addition to my healthcare practices.

None of that changes the point I'm making.

Whether you ever hire me, another billing company, or manage your billing entirely in-house is irrelevant to this discussion.

This post is not about selling services.

It's about raising awareness of an issue that affects healthcare providers across the country.

Insurance reimbursement should be transparent, accurate, and consistent with the applicable provider agreement and governing laws and regulations. When claims are reimbursed below the amount required by contract or applicable payment methodology, providers lose revenue they earned, practices face unnecessary financial strain, and ultimately patients can be affected when healthcare organizations have fewer resources to provide care.

Providers spend years learning medicine, nursing, and patient care. Very few receive formal education on how to verify that insurance companies are reimbursing claims correctly. This is a knowledge gap worth discussing.

My goal is to encourage providers to understand their reimbursements, ask questions, and verify that they are receiving the payments to which they are entitled. Whether they do that themselves, through their staff, or with outside assistance is entirely their decision.

Given the current commercial insurance landscape, providers are navigating a melting pot of inconsistent reimbursement methodologies, varying contractual obligations, opaque payment practices, and increasingly complex claims adjudication processes. Determining whether a claim was paid correctly has become far more difficult than simply confirming that a payment was received.

The greater challenge is determining whether a processed claim was reimbursed correctly.

An insurance payment isn't necessarily correct simply because the claim was processed and money was deposited.

To determine whether a claim was paid correctly, you need to know several things:

• Your contracted fee schedule with that specific payer.

• Whether the payer applied the correct allowable amount.

• Whether the correct CPT code was paid.

• Whether any contractual adjustments were appropriate.

• Whether any payer edits or reductions were applied correctly.

Most providers are never taught how to verify that an insurance payment matches their contracted reimbursement. As a result, once a claim is processed and payment is received, it is often assumed that the payer reimbursed the claim correctly even though that may not be the case.

Without routinely verifying reimbursement against contracted rates, underpayments can remain hidden for months or even years, gradually resulting in significant revenue loss.

A reimbursement difference of $20 or $30 on a commonly billed service may not seem significant. However, when that same difference occurs across hundreds or thousands of claims, it can result in a substantial loss of revenue.

This is why payment posting should never be viewed as the final step in the revenue cycle.

The real question is not simply, "Was the claim paid?"  It is, "Was the claim paid correctly according to the contract?"

Understanding the difference between a denied claim, a reduced payment, a contractual adjustment, and an actual underpayment is an important part of protecting the financial health of any medical practice.

The screenshots below illustrate an important point: the payment amount shown on an ERA is only one piece of the story. Without knowing the applicable reimbursement methodology or contracted allowable, it is often impossible to determine whether the payment was accurate.

Most providers are never taught how to verify that an insurance payment matches their contracted reimbursement. As a result, once a claim is processed and payment is received, it is often assumed that the payer reimbursed the claim correctly even though that may not be the case.

 

Without routinely verifying reimbursement against contracted rates, underpayments can remain hidden for months or even years, gradually resulting in significant revenue loss.

 

A reimbursement difference of $20 or $30 on a commonly billed service may not seem significant. However, when that same difference occurs across hundreds or thousands of claims, it can result in a substantial loss of revenue.

 

This is why payment posting should never be viewed as the final step in the revenue cycle.

 

The real question is not simply, "Was the claim paid?"  It is, "Was the claim paid correctly according to the contract?"

 

Understanding the difference between a denied claim, a reduced payment, a contractual adjustment, and an actual underpayment is an important part of protecting the financial health of any medical practice.

 

The screenshots below illustrate an important point: the payment amount shown on an ERA is only one piece of the story. Without knowing the applicable reimbursement methodology or contracted allowable, it is often impossible to determine whether the payment was accurate.
